prompt.text:
Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-11.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
Current data-driven approaches for low-light RAW image denoising struggle with a significant bottleneck: the shortage of paired noisy-clean training data. While noise synthesis is a promising alternative to collecting real-world pairs, existing synthesis methods suffer from high implementation complexity. Accurate noise generation typically demands laborious, sensor-specific calibration (e.g., system gain measurement using specific charts/lighting) and complex profiling of signal-independent noise (e.g., fitting statistical distributions or training intermediate neural networks). These preparation steps often take days and require expert human intervention, rendering the deployment of self-supervised denoising techniques resource-intensive and unscalable.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that the rigorous physical calibration currently deemed necessary for noise synthesis is largely redundant for training effective neural networks. Specifically, we posit that:
1.  **System Gain Tolerance:** Deep learning models are robust to slight inaccuracies in noise variance. Since system gain is physically constrained by quantum efficiency (which falls within a narrow, predictable range), we can "hypothesize" this value rather than measuring it, without introducing intensity bias.
2.  **Direct Sampling Validity:** Complex statistical profiling of read noise is unnecessary. The most accurate representation of signal-independent noise is the sensor data itself. Therefore, directly sampling captured dark frames is superior to fitting parametric models, which often fail to capture real-world noise diversity.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)
We propose a streamlined, "calibration-free" noise synthesis pipeline designed to reduce preparation time from days to roughly one hour. The approach focuses on two main components:

**1. Hypothesizing Signal-Dependent Noise (Shot Noise)**
Instead of performing laborious system gain calibration using flat-field images or test charts, we will implement a logic based on physical constraints.
*   We will derive the system gain by assuming a standard range for Quantum Efficiency (QE) combined with the user-designated Analog Gain.
*   Using this hypothesized gain, we will generate shot noise (Poisson distribution) and apply it to clean images. The intuition is that the network learns to denoise effectively even if the noise severity (variance) in training slightly differs from the ground truth, provided the mean intensity remains unbiased.

**2. Sampling Signal-Independent Noise (Read/Dark Noise)**
We will eliminate the need for statistical distribution fitting (e.g., Gaussian/Tukey) or training auxiliary generative networks.
*   **Data Collection:** We will collect a set of dark frames (images taken with the lens cap on) from the target sensor.
*   **Direct Injection:** These dark frames will be sampled directly to provide the signal-independent noise component (read noise, thermal noise, etc.).
*   **Dark Shading Correction:** We will compute the average of these dark frames to identify fixed pattern noise (dark shading). This map will be subtracted during the pipeline to prevent color bias, isolating the random noise components.
*   **Omission of Bit-Depth Expansion:** We explicitly propose to skip "High-Bit-Depth Noise Recovery" (HBNR). We argue that the low-bit nature of raw dark frames accurately encodes quantization noise, and artificially expanding bit-depth adds unnecessary complexity and potential modeling errors.

## Expected Contribution
We aim to establish a new baseline for practical, self-supervised RAW image denoising. Theoretically, this work will demonstrate that neural networks possess an inherent robustness to approximate physical noise parameters, challenging the dogma that precise sensor calibration is mandatory. Practically, this pipeline will democratize low-light denoising by allowing users to train high-performance models for new camera sensors using only a quick, automated collection of dark frames, thereby removing the need for specialized laboratory equipment or extensive engineering time.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We designed a self-supervised RAW image denoising framework that eliminates the need for extensive calibration and noise profiling. The following setup details were used to generate the empirical results.

*   **Datasets:**
    *   **SID (Sony-A7S2):** Full-frame DSLR data. Test data included ISO values ranging from 100 to 25600.
    *   **ELD (Sony-A7S2):** Full-frame DSLR data. Test data included ISO values ranging from 100 to 25600.
    *   **LRID (Redmi K30):** Smartphone data captured with a 1/2.55 inch IMX686 sensor. Test data fixed at ISO 6400.
    *   **Dark Frame Sources:**
        *   For SID and ELD (which lack released dark frames), we utilized LLD calibration data (approx. 400 dark frames per ISO, 24 ISOs total).
        *   For LRID, we utilized the provided 360 dark frames (180 normal, 180 hot).
*   **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   PSNR (Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio)
    *   SSIM (Structural Similarity Index Measure)
*   **Baselines Compared:**
    *   **Supervised:** Paired data (Vanilla), PMN.
    *   **Hybrid:** LED, LLD.
    *   **Self-supervised:** Poisson-Gaussian (P-G), ELD, SFRN, NoiseFlow, StarLight, PNNP.
*   **Implementation Details:**
    *   **Backbone:** U-Net.
    *   **Input Size:** Random crops of $512 \times 512$ patches.
    *   **Optimization:** L1-loss minimization using an Adam optimizer.
    *   **Training Schedule:** 1000 epochs total (400 epochs for finetuning).
    *   **Augmentation:** Random vertical and horizontal flipping.
    *   **System Gain ($K$) Estimation:** Instead of calibration, we used a hypothesized QE of 40%. The empirical approximation was $K = (\text{ISO} / 100) \times 0.1$.
    *   **Dark Shading:** We employed dark shadings provided by PMN for fair comparison across all methods.
    *   **Inference:** Dark shading was subtracted from the noisy image before inputting it to the network.

## 3. Qualitative Observations

*   **Preparation Efficiency:** We observed that our method requires only "one hour" (specifically for dark frame collection), whereas comparative methods require "hours to days" for system gain calibration and noise profiling.
*   **Pipeline Simplification:** We found that hypothesizing system gain for shot noise and using direct dark frame sampling for signal-independent noise is sufficient for high performance.
*   **Visual Quality:** In visual comparisons against ELD and SFRN methods, our output avoided the noticeable color bias along image boundaries exhibited by the baseline methods. Our results were visually comparable to the ground truth.
*   **Performance Gain:** We achieved an up to 0.54dB PSNR improvement over the state-of-the-art self-supervised method (PNNP).
*   **Profiling Accuracy (Q-Q Plots):**
    *   We observed that the Tukey-Lambda distribution failed to fully capture the true noise distribution of the training data.
    *   We observed that Gaussian Mixture Models (GMM) fit the training data perfectly but exhibited deviations when tested against unseen dark frames, indicating poor generalization.
*   **Robustness to Gain ($K$):** We determined that denoising networks are robust to the system gain $K$. Varying $K$ significantly (e.g., up to a factor of 2 or random sampling) resulted in PSNR differences smaller than 0.1 dB.
*   **Robustness to Shading Calibration:** We observed that the method is robust to the number of dark frames used for shading calibration in inference. Using only 10 dark frames caused a drop of only 0.1 dB compared to using 180 frames. Even with 2 frames, our method outperformed existing self-supervised approaches.
*   **Data Efficiency:** We found that high performance is maintained even when reducing the training data to only 10 dark frames per ISO (approx. 0.1 dB PSNR decrease).
*   **HBNR Redundancy:** We concluded that High-Bit-Depth Noise Recovery (HBNR) is unnecessary. The performance difference with and without HBNR was less than 0.1 dB across all datasets.
*   **Sensor Heating:** We attributed the performance improvement over profiling methods partly to the ability of direct sampling to capture noise variations caused by sensor heating, which static profiling misses.

Role: Senior AI Researcher and Academic Writer.
Objective: Complete a machine learning research paper by filling in missing sections of a provided LaTeX template and generating a corresponding bibliography file. You must produce a scientifically sound, well-structured paper suitable for submission to a top-tier ML conference.

Inputs
You will receive the following materials:
• idea.md: Detailed description of the proposed method and technical ideas.
• experimental_log.md: Raw experimental results and observations used to construct tables, figures, and analysis.
• conference_guidelines.md: Formatting and stylistic requirements for the target conference.
• figures_list: A list of figures that may be referenced in the paper.

Conference Guidelines
# CVPR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the latex paper writing process for CVPR 2025.

## Language
All manuscripts must be in English.

## Submission Policies & Anonymity
CVPR reviewing is double-blind. Authors must not know the names of the reviewers, and reviewers must not know the names of the authors.

* **No Identifying Information:** Do not provide information that may identify the authors in the acknowledgments (e.g., co-workers and grant IDs) or in the supplementary material.
* **Links:** Do not provide links to websites that identify the authors.
* **GitHub:** Links to GitHub must be anonymous.
* **Self-Citation:** If you need to cite any of your own papers that are being submitted concurrently, include anonymized versions in the supplementary material and cite them as anonymous. Do not use the words "my" or "our" when citing previous work; treat your own prior work as if it were written by someone else (e.g., "Smith et al. showed..." rather than "We showed...").

## Paper length
Papers, excluding the references section, must be no longer than eight pages in length.
The references section will not be included in the page count, and there is no limit on the length of the references section.
For example, a paper of eight pages with two pages of references would have a total length of 10 pages.

Overlength papers, or papers where margins and formatting are deemed significantly altered, will simply not be reviewed.

## Mathematics
Please number all of your sections and displayed equations as in these examples:
```latex
\begin{equation}
  E = m\cdot c^2
  \label{eq:important}
\end{equation}
```
and
```latex
\begin{equation}
  v = a\cdot t.
  \label{eq:also-important}
\end{equation}
```

## Formatting your paper
All text must be in a two-column format.
The total allowable size of the text area is $6\frac78$ inches (17.46 cm) wide by $8\frac78$ inches (22.54 cm) high.
Columns are to be $3\frac14$ inches (8.25 cm) wide, with a $\frac{5}{16}$ inch (0.8 cm) space between them.
The main title (on the first page) should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge of the page.
The second and following pages should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge.
On all pages, the bottom margin should be $1\frac{1}{8}$ inches (2.86 cm) from the bottom edge of the page for $8.5 \times 11$-inch paper;
for A4 paper, approximately $1\frac{5}{8}$ inches (4.13 cm) from the bottom edge of the page.

### Type style and fonts
Wherever Times is specified, Times Roman may also be used. If neither is available on your word processor, please use the font closest in appearance to Times to which you have access.

### Main Title
Center the title $1\frac{3}{8}$ inches (3.49 cm) from the top edge of the first page. The title should be in Times 14-point, boldface type. Capitalize the first letter of nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs; do not capitalize articles, coordinate conjunctions, or prepositions (unless the title begins with such a word).

The ABSTRACT and MAIN TEXT are to be in a two-column format.

### Main Text
Type main text in 10-point Times, single-spaced.
Do NOT use double-spacing.
All paragraphs should be indented 1 pica (approx.~$\frac{1}{6}$ inch or 0.422 cm). Make sure your text is fully justified---that is, flush left and flush right. Please do not place any additional blank lines between paragraphs.

Figure and table captions should be 9-point Roman type as in \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short}. 
Short captions should be centred.

\noindent Callouts should be 9-point Helvetica, non-boldface type. Initially capitalize only the first word of section titles and first-, second-, and third-order headings.

#### First-order Headings
For example, {\large \bf 1. Introduction} should be Times 12-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one blank line after.

#### Second-order Headings
For example, { \bf 1.1. Database elements} should be Times 11-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one after.
If you require a third-order heading (we discourage it), use 10-point Times, boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, preceded by one blank line, followed by a period and your text on the same line.

### Footnotes
Please use \footnote{This is what a footnote looks like.
It often distracts the reader from the main flow of the argument.} sparingly.

Indeed, try to avoid footnotes altogether and include necessary peripheral observations in the text (within parentheses, if you prefer, as in this sentence). If you wish to use a footnote, place it at the bottom of the column on the page on which it is referenced.
Use Times 8-point type, single-spaced.

### Cross-references
For the benefit of author(s) and readers, please use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
```
command for cross-referencing to figures, tables, equations, or sections.

This will automatically insert the appropriate label alongside the cross-reference as in this example:
```latex
\begin{quotation}
  To see how our method outperforms previous work, please see \cref{fig:onecol} and \cref{tab:example}.
  It is also possible to refer to multiple targets as once, \eg~to \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short-a}.
  You may also return to \cref{sec:formatting} or look at \cref{eq:also-important}.
\end{quotation}
```
If you do not wish to abbreviate the label, for example at the beginning of the sentence, you can use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \Cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
command. Here is an example:
\begin{quotation}
  \Cref{fig:onecol} is also quite important.
\end{quotation}
```

## Example Code for Tables

references.text:
## Problem Statement
The current landscape of data-driven low-light RAW image denoising is bifurcated into supervised methods, which require impractical paired real-world data, and self-supervised methods based on noise synthesis. While noise synthesis offers a scalable path, existing techniques suffer from a critical bottleneck: they necessitate labor-intensive calibration and profiling procedures.

Specifically, current state-of-the-art synthesis pipelines require:
1.  **Precise System Gain Calibration:** This demands collecting flat-field images or standard noise test charts under strictly controlled lighting to model signal-dependent noise. This hardware setup can take days to configure, particularly for irregular devices like endoscopes.
2.  **Signal-Independent Noise Profiling:** This involves complex statistical justifications (e.g., fitting specific distributions) or training intermediate "profiling neural networks."
3.  **High-Bit-Depth Noise Recovery (HBNR):** A complex process used to mitigate quantization noise by expanding the bit-depth of dark frames, which re-necessitates statistical profiling.

These requirements render the deployment of self-supervised denoising resource-intensive and slow. We aim to solve the problem of high "preparation cost" without sacrificing the physical accuracy of the noise model.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that the rigorous calibration of system gain and the statistical profiling of signal-independent noise are redundant for training effective denoising networks.

Our core technical postulates are:
1.  **Hypothesized Gain Sufficiency:** The system gain $K$ is physically constrained by Quantum Efficiency (QE), which varies within a small, predictable range. Therefore, we can synthesize signal-dependent noise by *hypothesizing* the QE rather than measuring it, effectively treating gain variation as a form of data augmentation.
2.  **Direct Sensor Sampling:** Explicit statistical modeling of read noise (signal-independent) introduces bias. We posit that directly sampling dark frames from the sensor—without bit-depth expansion or parametric modeling—provides a more accurate and simpler representation of the true noise distribution.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

### 1. Image Formation Model
We will adopt a rigorous physics-based image formation model to ground our synthesis pipeline. We define the conversion from incident photons to digital pixel values $D$ as:

$$ D = \underbrace { K _ { a } \left( X + N _ { p } \right) } _ { \mathrm { s i g n a l - d e p e n d e n t } } + \underbrace { K _ { a } N _ { 1 } + N _ { 2 } } _ { \mathrm { s i g n a l - i n d e p e n d e n t } } $$

Where:
*   $K_a$ is the analog system gain.
*   $X$ is the real number of photons (proportional to scene irradiance).
*   $N_p$ is signal-dependent photon shot noise.
*   $N_1$ is pre-amplification signal-independent noise (e.g., dark current, thermal noise).
*   $N_2$ is post-amplification noise (e.g., quantization noise, banding noise).
*   We assume digital gain $K_d = 1$ for simplicity.

### 2. Hypothesizing Signal-Dependent Noise
Instead of calibrating $K_a$ via flat-field frames, we will derive it theoretically. We observe that system gain is the product of Quantum Efficiency (QE) and Analog Gain (AG):
$$ \operatorname { S y s t e m } \operatorname { g a i n } K = \operatorname { Q E } \times \operatorname { A G } $$

Since AG is user-designated and known, and QE typically ranges between 30% and 70% for modern silicon, we will hypothesize a fixed QE (e.g., 50%) to estimate $K$.

We will synthesize the noisy signal by sampling from a Poisson distribution scaled by this hypothesized gain. The generation process for a clean image $I$ (where $I = K_a X$) will be:
$$ \begin{array} { r } { \left( X + N _ { p } \right) \sim \mathcal { P } \left( I / K _ { a } \right) } \\ { \Rightarrow K _ { a } \left( X + N _ { p } \right) \sim K _ { a } \mathcal { P } \left( I / K _ { a } \right) } \end{array} $$

We assert that errors in the hypothesized $K$ only affect noise *severity* (variance), not the intensity bias (mean), as shown by:
$$ \mathbb { E } \left( K \left( X + N _ { p } \right) \right) = K \cdot I / K = I $$
$$ \mathbb { V } \left( K \left( X + N _ { p } \right) \right) = K ^ { 2 } \cdot I / K = K I $$
Thus, the network will not learn incorrect color biases even if the gain is imprecise.

### 3. Sampling Signal-Independent Noise (Dark Frame Strategy)
We will eliminate parametric modeling (Gaussian/Tukey-Lambda fitting) and intermediate networks (GANs/Flows). Instead, we will implement a **Direct Sampling** strategy:
1.  **Collection:** We will collect a bank of dark frames (captured with the lens cap on) for the target sensor.
2.  **Dark Shading Correction:** We will compute the "dark shading" pattern by averaging multiple dark frames to isolate fixed pattern noise.
    *   *Inference:* This fixed pattern will be subtracted from the input noisy image.
    *   *Training:* We will subtract this fixed pattern from our sampled dark frames to isolate the temporal stochastic noise, ensuring the network learns to handle random noise variations.
3.  **Synthesis Integration:** We will directly add these processed dark frames to the synthetic shot noise generated in Step 2.

**Exclusion of HBNR:** We explicitly plan to omit High-Bit-Depth Noise Recovery (HBNR). We argue that low-bit dark frames accurately depict real-world quantization noise, and fitting distributions to expand bit-depth introduces unnecessary complexity and potential modeling errors.

### 4. Training Configuration
*   **Backbone:** We will utilize a standard U-Net architecture.
*   **Input:** Synthetic noisy images generated by combining hypothesized shot noise and sampled dark frames.
*   **Loss Function:** We will minimize the L1 loss between the network prediction and the clean ground truth.
*   **Augmentation:** We will treat the hypothesized system gain as a data augmentation parameter, training the network to be robust across a range of noise levels.

## Expected Contribution
1.  **Operational Efficiency:** We expect to reduce the preparation time for sensor-specific noise synthesis from days to approximately one hour (the time required to capture dark frames), automating the process entirely.
2.  **Simplification of Pipeline:** We will demonstrate that laborious steps—specifically system gain calibration, parametric noise profiling, and bit-depth expansion—are theoretically redundant for learning-based denoising.
3.  **Robustness by Design:** By deriving our method from the physical limitations of Quantum Efficiency and direct sensor sampling, we expect the model to be robust to gain variations and free from the domain gaps introduced by over-simplified statistical noise assumptions (e.g., Gaussian assumptions).

notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).

preinstalled.en: python:3.11 bookworm; upstream code via PYTHONPATH; pdflatex + bibtex; CPU PyTorch with numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib and more (pinned by constraints.txt)

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

preinstalled.zh: 上游锁定依赖（uv sync --frozen）加兼容补丁 compat.patch；TeX Live（含 fonts-extra、latexmk）；给 agent 用的研究 Python 环境 /opt/research
preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
